question.question:
D1 — Use the job library's retry hook or roll a custom inline scheduler?
Project/branch/task: main branch of the retry-framework plan; the plan currently bypasses the existing job library's retry hooks in 5 workers.
ELI10: The job library you already run knows how to retry a failed job: it counts attempts, waits, re-queues, and gives up after a limit. The plan rewrites that logic by hand inside every worker because the team wants to shape the wait-time curve. Most libraries let you pass your own curve to the built-in retry, so hand-rolling buys little and loses the library's bookkeeping.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a hand-rolled scheduler owns attempt counting, dead-lettering and crash recovery itself; a bug there means jobs retry forever or vanish silently, in five places, and the library's dashboards and metrics stop telling the truth.
Recommendation: A because the plan itself says the custom version is "same shape" as the library's, and a backoff callback gives full control of the curve without re-owning retry state.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=6/10, C=n/a (investigation only)
Pros / cons:
A) Library hook + custom backoff callback (recommended)
  ✅ Library keeps attempt counting, max tries, dead-letter routing and crash recovery; one tested code path instead of five new ones
  ✅ Curve is still fully yours: exponent, cap and jitter live in one callback that is trivial to unit test (human: ~1 day / CC: ~10 min)
  ❌ If the library's hook turns out not to accept a custom curve, you spend a short probe before falling back to a custom scheduler
B) Custom inline scheduler as planned
  ✅ No dependency on the library's hook API or its release cadence; the team controls every line
  ✅ Can express curves or side effects the hook cannot, if such a need exists
  ❌ Re-owns attempt counting, persistence across worker crashes and dead-lettering in 5 workers; high blast radius for a 3am bug (human: ~1 week / CC: ~45 min plus tests)
C) Probe the library hook first, decide after
  ✅ Replaces an assumption with evidence: one read of the retry config API settles whether a backoff callback is supported
  ✅ Bounded: one hour human / a few CC minutes; no implementation changes until the answer lands
  ❌ Delays the decision; everything downstream (envelope sharing, tests) waits on it
Net: trade a short API probe and a thin callback against re-owning retry state in five workers.

The library keeps attempt counting, max tries, dead-letter routing and crash recovery. Fall back to a custom scheduler only if a probe proves the hook cannot express the curve. Completeness 9/10. Effort: human ~1 day / CC ~10 min. Backoff shape, envelope sharing (R2), webhook semantics (R3) and graph caching (R4) stay pending.

The team re-owns attempt counting, persistence across crashes and dead-lettering. Completeness 6/10. Effort: human ~1 week / CC ~45 min plus tests. Backoff shape, R2, R3 and R4 stay pending.

question.question:
D2 — What delivery guarantee does the webhook job keep once retries exist, and what test proves it?
Project/branch/task: main branch of the retry-framework plan; `processWebhookJob()` is being rewritten under the newly approved library retry hook (D1).
ELI10: Today a webhook fires at most once: if it fails, it is not sent again, so receivers never see duplicates. A retry framework re-runs failed jobs, which by definition can send the same webhook twice. The plan rewrites the webhook job without saying which behavior receivers should get, and plans no test to prove it. We need to pick the guarantee and lock it with a regression test before the rewrite.
Stakes if we pick wrong: external receivers either start getting duplicate webhooks they never deduped (double charges, double notifications) or the team believes retries protect webhooks when they do not; either failure is silent because nothing tests it.
Recommendation: A because it preserves the contract receivers already rely on, still lets retries cover transient pre-send failures, and keeps a later move to at-least-once a separate, reversible decision.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Keep at-most-once; retry only before send (recommended)
  ✅ Receivers see no behavior change; no coordination with external consumers or idempotency rollout needed
  ✅ Transient failures while loading the payload or building the graph still get retried; three regression tests pin the contract (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min)
  ❌ A webhook whose HTTP send fails stays failed and dead-lettered; operators must replay it by hand
B) Move to at-least-once with an idempotency key
  ✅ Send failures self-heal through the retry curve; this is how most webhook platforms behave
  ✅ A per-job idempotency key gives receivers a clean way to dedupe, and tests pin key stability across attempts
  ❌ It is a receiver-facing contract change: every consumer must dedupe on the key before this ships, or they get duplicates (human: ~1 week incl. consumer outreach / CC: ~30 min code)
C) Investigate receivers and the current job first
  ✅ Replaces guesses about receiver dedupe behavior and the current send path with evidence
  ✅ Bounded: read `processWebhookJob()` and the receiver list (human: ~half day / CC: ~5 min)
  ❌ The guarantee and its tests stay undecided; the rewrite cannot start safely until this returns
Net: preserve the existing promise and retry only the safe half of the job, or change the promise and pay the consumer-coordination cost up front.

options.label: Keep at-most-once; retry only before send (recommended)
options.description: Library retry applies only to failures before the HTTP send is attempted; the send stage runs with max attempts 1 or checks a persisted "dispatching" marker so a crash after send does not re-send. Required regression tests: failure after send → exactly one HTTP call and the job is failed/dead-lettered, not re-queued; failure before send → retried per the curve; simulated crash between send and ack → no second send. Effort: human ~1 day / CC ~15 min. R2, R4 and R5 stay pending.

options.label: Move to at-least-once with an idempotency key
options.description: Webhook retried on send failure under the library curve, with a stable per-job (not per-attempt) idempotency key in the request; receiver-facing contract change documented. Required tests: send failure → retried with an identical key on every attempt; key stable across process restart; exhausted attempts → dead-letter. Effort: human ~1 week including consumer outreach / CC ~30 min code. R2, R4 and R5 stay pending.

options.label: Investigate receivers and the current job first
options.description: Bounded investigation only: read `processWebhookJob()` and audit receivers for dedupe behavior (human ~half day / CC ~5 min), then return to this question. Approves no implementation or tests; the guarantee, R2, R4 and R5 stay pending.

question.question:
D3 — How many times may a job retry, and what happens when it runs out?
Project/branch/task: main branch of the retry-framework plan; retries now run under the library hook (D1) with the webhook send excluded (D2).
ELI10: Exponential backoff only says how long to wait between tries, not how many tries. Without a limit, a job that can never succeed (bad payload, deleted record) keeps coming back forever and floods the queue; with a limit but no landing spot, it just disappears when the limit is hit. The plan says nothing about either.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a poison job retries indefinitely and starves real work, or failed jobs vanish silently and nobody notices customers' work never happened.
Recommendation: A because bounded attempts plus a dead-letter queue with an alert is the standard, boring shape, and the library already provides it under D1.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=4/10
Pros / cons:
A) Bounded attempts, dead-letter, alert (recommended)
  ✅ Poison jobs stop after a known number of tries and land somewhere an operator can inspect and replay; attempt history is logged with them
  ✅ A metric or alert on dead-letter growth turns silent failure into a page; one config line per job type (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
  ❌ Each job type needs a sensible attempt count and someone has to own the dead-letter queue
B) Leave it to library defaults, plan stays silent
  ✅ Zero extra work now; the library's default limit applies if it has one
  ✅ No new operational surface (no dead-letter queue to watch) in this change
  ❌ Nobody has verified the default; it may be unlimited or silent-drop, and the plan would ship a retry framework with no defined end state
Net: a few config lines and an alert now versus discovering the exhaustion behavior in production.

options.label: Bounded attempts, dead-letter, alert (recommended)
options.description: Plan names a default max-attempt count per job type (implementer tunes), exhausted jobs go to the library's dead-letter route with their attempt history logged, and a metric/alert fires on dead-letter growth. Max delay cap is derived from base × 2^attempts and documented. Completeness 9/10. Effort: human ~half day / CC ~10 min. R2, R4 and R6 stay pending.

options.label: Leave it to library defaults, plan stays silent
options.description: Keep the plan as written: no attempt limit, no dead-letter behavior and no alert specified; whatever the library does by default applies. Completeness 4/10. Effort: none. R2, R4 and R6 stay pending.

question.question:
D4 — One shared retry-policy module, or five inline copies refactored "later"?
Project/branch/task: main branch of the retry-framework plan; with D1 the library owns re-dispatch, so what is left per worker is the curve callback, the per-job policy and attempt logging.
ELI10: The plan copies the same retry wrapper into five worker files and promises to clean it up later. Later rarely comes, and five copies means five places to fix when the curve or the logging is wrong. With the library hook doing the heavy lifting, the shared part is small: one curve function, one table of per-job settings, one logging hook.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a curve bug or a logging gap gets fixed in four files and missed in the fifth, and the next job type copies whichever version its author found first.
Recommendation: A because five plan-stated callers with identical behavior clear the shared-code bar, the helper is tiny, and extracting before the behavior change keeps the refactor and the feature separate.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=4/10
Pros / cons:
A) One shared retry-policy module (recommended)
  ✅ Curve, per-job attempt limits and attempt logging live in one tested place; adding a sixth job type is a one-line policy entry
  ✅ Roughly 50-110 fewer implementation lines than five copies, and the refactor lands before the behavior change (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min)
  ❌ A bug in the shared callback hits all five job types at once, so the module needs its own unit tests
B) Five inline copies, refactor later
  ✅ Each worker is self-contained and readable without jumping to a shared file
  ✅ No shared-failure blast radius; a mistake stays inside one job type
  ❌ Five copies of the same logic drift; the plan already calls this "duplicated" and defers the fix with no owner or trigger
Net: a small shared module with tests now, or five copies and a refactor nobody has scheduled.

options.label: One shared retry-policy module (recommended)
options.description: Extract one module holding the backoff callback, a per-job-type policy table (max attempts per D3, webhook send stage excluded per D2) and one attempt-logging hook registered at queue level. Each of the 5 workers declares its policy in a few lines; no copy-pasted envelope remains. Shared-module unit tests are required proof. Completeness 9/10. Effort: human ~1 day / CC ~15 min. R4, R6 and R7 stay pending.

options.label: Five inline copies, refactor later
options.description: Keep the plan as written: each worker carries its own callback invocation, policy constants and attempt logging; refactor deferred with no trigger. Completeness 4/10. Effort: human ~0 extra now / CC ~0, debt carried. R4, R6 and R7 stay pending.

question.question:
D5 — Should permanent errors skip the retry curve and dead-letter immediately?
Project/branch/task: main branch of the retry-framework plan; retries live in the shared policy module (D4) under the library hook (D1) with bounded attempts (D3).
ELI10: Some failures fix themselves if you wait, like a database hiccup. Others never will, like a payload that fails validation or a record that was deleted. Retrying the second kind just wastes every attempt and delays the moment someone notices. The plan treats all failures the same.
Stakes if we pick wrong: permanent failures sit in the queue for the whole backoff window before anyone sees them, and the queue spends worker time on jobs that cannot succeed; or, if classification is wrong, a transient error is mislabeled permanent and a recoverable job is dead-lettered early.
Recommendation: A because the shared module already exists under D4, the classification is a small predicate, and it turns a slow silent failure into an immediate visible one.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=6/10
Pros / cons:
A) Classify: permanent errors dead-letter immediately (recommended)
  ✅ Bad payloads and missing records surface in the dead-letter queue on the first attempt with the reason attached, instead of after the full curve
  ✅ Worker time and the attempt budget go to failures that can actually recover; the predicate is one function in the shared module with its own tests (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
  ❌ A misclassified transient error gets dead-lettered early; the predicate must default to retry when unsure
B) Retry everything until the attempt bound
  ✅ Simplest rule, no error taxonomy to maintain across five job types
  ✅ No risk of mislabeling a recoverable error as permanent
  ❌ Permanent failures consume every attempt and the full backoff window before dead-lettering; a bad deploy fills the queue with hopeless retries
Net: a small, retry-by-default predicate in the shared module versus burning the full curve on errors that can never succeed.

options.label: Classify: permanent errors dead-letter immediately (recommended)
options.description: The shared policy module gains a retryable predicate: validation errors, not-found and non-retryable 4xx-class responses go straight to dead-letter with the reason; everything else follows the curve. Default is retry when unsure. Unit tests cover both branches (required proof). Completeness 9/10. Effort: human ~half day / CC ~10 min. R4 and R6 stay pending.

options.label: Retry everything until the attempt bound
options.description: Every failure follows the D3 curve until attempts are exhausted, then dead-letters. No error taxonomy. Completeness 6/10. Effort: none. R4 and R6 stay pending.

# Eng review: Add background job retry framework

Report destination requested by the user. Review target (fixed): `PLAN.md` in

("Plan: Add background job retry framework"). Reviewer: /plan-eng-review,
session 702-1791142398-ec68c409, branch main, commit e767d72.

## Original plan (unchanged copy)

```markdown
# Plan: Add background job retry framework

## Architecture
We'll roll a custom exponential-backoff scheduler inline in each worker
rather than use the existing job library's built-in retry hooks. Same
shape as the library version, but we want full control over the curve.

## Code quality
The retry envelope (compute delay, log attempt, dispatch) is duplicated
across 5 worker files with copy-pasted bodies. We will leave the
duplication for now and refactor "later."

## Tests
The existing `processWebhookJob()` flow gets rewritten as part of this
change. No regression test for the prior at-most-once delivery guarantee
is planned.

## Performance
On every retry we re-fetch the full job payload from the database, then
iterate the payload to recompute the dependency graph. Could cache the
graph on the first attempt; not planned.
```

## Scope Challenge — assessment

**Evidence available.** The review repo contains only `CLAUDE.md` and `PLAN.md`.
The five worker files, `processWebhookJob()`, the job library and its retry hooks
are named by the plan but are `not available` in this checkout. Every finding
below is calibrated against the plan text (file:line) plus industry practice;
runtime behavior of the existing code is unknown.

**What already solves each sub-problem.**
- Exponential backoff scheduling: the plan says the existing job library already
  ships retry hooks and the custom version is "same shape" (PLAN.md:7-9). Reuse
  ladder rung 4 (already-installed dependency). Whether the hooks accept a custom
  backoff function is unknown; typical libraries (BullMQ, Sidekiq, Oban, Laravel
  queues, Celery) do.
- Retry envelope (compute delay, log attempt, dispatch): no shared helper exists
  per the plan; five proposed copies (PLAN.md:12-14).
- Delivery guarantee: today `processWebhookJob()` is at-most-once (PLAN.md:17-19).
  Any retry layer turns it into at-least-once unless dispatch is excluded or
  deduped.

**Minimum change that achieves the goal.** Configure the library's retry hook with
a custom curve; one small envelope helper for the five workers only if the library
hook cannot own the envelope; settle webhook delivery semantics explicitly and
cover them with a regression test; compute the dependency graph once per job.

**Complexity check (estimates).** Proposed changed files: 5 worker files, plus 0-1
new helper module. New classes/services: 0-1 (a scheduler/helper). Below the
8-file / 2-class gate, so Scope Challenge B is skipped.

**Search check.** Aside not installed; host WebSearch used (one read-only query,
sanitized). Consensus: use the queue library's declarative retry/backoff with
jitter and a max-attempt cap, route exhausted jobs to a dead-letter queue, and
treat duplicates as policy under at-least-once, so side effects need idempotency
keys. Sources:
[DEV: Node.js job queue retry/ack/idempotency](https://dev.to/thomasmoore157/how-to-build-a-nodejs-background-job-queue-retry-ack-and-idempotency-59ea),
[Berkanium: job queues done right](https://www.berkanium.net/articles/job-queues-done-right),
[Moments Log: retry policy checklist](https://www.momentslog.com/development/background-job-retry-policy-checklist-how-to-prevent-queues-from-amplifying-production-failures),
[benmoataz: idempotent job queue](https://www.benmoataz.com/posts/idempotent-job-queue/),
[Laravel queue best practices](https://dev.to/laravelo11y/laravel-background-jobs-12-best-practices-for-production-queues-5gcm).
Layering: library retry hooks are **[Layer 1]**; a hand-rolled inline scheduler
is **[Layer 3]** with no first-principles reason given beyond "control over the
curve", which a backoff callback already provides.

**TODOS cross-reference.** No `TODOS.md` in the repo.

**Completeness check.** A regression test for at-most-once delivery and a cached
dependency graph each cost CC minutes; both are deferred in the plan.

**Distribution check.** No new artifacts; nothing to publish.

   scheduling inline in each worker although it admits the result is "same shape"
   as the built-in; "full control over the curve" is normally a backoff callback
   on the existing hook, not a reason to bypass the library's attempt counting,
   dead-lettering and visibility.` Motivating lines: "We'll roll a custom
   exponential-backoff scheduler inline in each worker rather than use the
   existing job library's built-in retry hooks. Same shape as the library
   version, but we want full control over the curve." Not 9/10 because the
   library is not in this checkout, so whether its hook accepts a custom curve

Related findings on duplication, delivery semantics and per-retry refetch are
handled in Sections 2, 1/3 and 4 respectively; the first depends on R1's answer.

Finding: Section 1 (Architecture) #2, P2, confidence 8/10, PLAN.md:6-9, reviewer: plan-eng-review (Claude)

| Choice | Current | A | B |
|---|---|---|---|
| R5 exhaustion policy | unspecified; plan silent | bounded attempts (plan names a default, implementer tunes per job type) then dead-letter with attempt history logged and a metric/alert on dead-letter growth | leave to the library's default; plan stays silent |
| Max delay cap | implied only by attempt count | derived: base × 2^attempts, chosen so the last wait is acceptable; documented in plan | unspecified |
| R1 mechanism (D1), R3 guarantee (D2) | approved | unchanged | unchanged |
| R2 envelope sharing, R4 graph caching, R6 jitter | pending | pending | pending |

Question D3:
D3 — How many times may a job retry, and what happens when it runs out?
Project/branch/task: main branch of the retry-framework plan; retries now run under the library hook (D1) with the webhook send excluded (D2).
ELI10: Exponential backoff only says how long to wait between tries, not how many tries. Without a limit, a job that can never succeed (bad payload, deleted record) keeps coming back forever and floods the queue; with a limit but no landing spot, it just disappears when the limit is hit. The plan says nothing about either.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a poison job retries indefinitely and starves real work, or failed jobs vanish silently and nobody notices customers' work never happened.
Recommendation: A because bounded attempts plus a dead-letter queue with an alert is the standard, boring shape, and the library already provides it under D1.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=4/10
Pros / cons:
A) Bounded attempts, dead-letter, alert (recommended)
  ✅ Poison jobs stop after a known number of tries and land somewhere an operator can inspect and replay; attempt history is logged with them
  ✅ A metric or alert on dead-letter growth turns silent failure into a page; one config line per job type (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
  ❌ Each job type needs a sensible attempt count and someone has to own the dead-letter queue
B) Leave it to library defaults, plan stays silent
  ✅ Zero extra work now; the library's default limit applies if it has one
  ✅ No new operational surface (no dead-letter queue to watch) in this change
  ❌ Nobody has verified the default; it may be unlimited or silent-drop, and the plan would ship a retry framework with no defined end state
Net: a few config lines and an alert now versus discovering the exhaustion behavior in production.

Finding: Section 2 (Code quality) #2, P2, confidence 7/10, PLAN.md:6-9 and 12-14, reviewer: plan-eng-review (Claude)

|---|---|---|---|
| R7 error classification | retry every failure until exhaustion (implicit) | shared policy module distinguishes permanent errors (validation, not-found, non-retryable 4xx) from transient ones; permanent errors go straight to dead-letter with the reason, transient ones follow the curve | retry every failure until the D3 attempt bound, then dead-letter |
| R1, R2, R3, R5 (approved D1-D4) | approved | unchanged | unchanged |
| R4 graph caching, R6 jitter | pending | pending | pending |

Question D5:
D5 — Should permanent errors skip the retry curve and dead-letter immediately?
Project/branch/task: main branch of the retry-framework plan; retries live in the shared policy module (D4) under the library hook (D1) with bounded attempts (D3).
ELI10: Some failures fix themselves if you wait, like a database hiccup. Others never will, like a payload that fails validation or a record that was deleted. Retrying the second kind just wastes every attempt and delays the moment someone notices. The plan treats all failures the same.
Stakes if we pick wrong: permanent failures sit in the queue for the whole backoff window before anyone sees them, and the queue spends worker time on jobs that cannot succeed; or, if classification is wrong, a transient error is mislabeled permanent and a recoverable job is dead-lettered early.
Recommendation: A because the shared module already exists under D4, the classification is a small predicate, and it turns a slow silent failure into an immediate visible one.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=6/10
Pros / cons:
A) Classify: permanent errors dead-letter immediately (recommended)
  ✅ Bad payloads and missing records surface in the dead-letter queue on the first attempt with the reason attached, instead of after the full curve
  ✅ Worker time and the attempt budget go to failures that can actually recover; the predicate is one function in the shared module with its own tests (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
  ❌ A misclassified transient error gets dead-lettered early; the predicate must default to retry when unsure
B) Retry everything until the attempt bound
  ✅ Simplest rule, no error taxonomy to maintain across five job types
  ✅ No risk of mislabeling a recoverable error as permanent
  ❌ Permanent failures consume every attempt and the full backoff window before dead-lettering; a bad deploy fills the queue with hopeless retries
Net: a small, retry-by-default predicate in the shared module versus burning the full curve on errors that can never succeed.
Header: Error classes

A) Classify: permanent errors dead-letter immediately (recommended)
The shared policy module gains a retryable predicate: validation errors, not-found and non-retryable 4xx-class responses go straight to dead-letter with the reason; everything else follows the curve. Default is retry when unsure. Unit tests cover both branches (required proof). Completeness 9/10. Effort: human ~half day / CC ~10 min. R4 and R6 stay pending.
B) Retry everything until the attempt bound
Every failure follows the D3 curve until attempts are exhausted, then dead-letters. No error taxonomy. Completeness 6/10. Effort: none. R4 and R6 stay pending.
